intro: The tension between AI's accelerating pace and the public's growing pushback is front and center today: METR's unprecedented look inside Anthropic suggests AI progress is running at double speed — with AI itself driving most of the acceleration — while protesters scale cranes at Microsoft data centers, OpenAI scrambles to rebuild trust after midterm losses, and white-collar workers quit jobs over fears that haven't materialized yet. We've also got Amazon betting big on an AI shopping agent just in time for the holidays, a decade-old SSH vulnerability that could affect billions of Docker containers, and a startup sending humanoid robots in grippy socks to clean San Francisco apartments for $60 a week.

stories.title: Amazon launches text-based Alexa shopping agent ahead of holiday season
stories.summary: Amazon is rolling out a text-based Alexa shopping agent that lets US customers search for products, compare items, add to cart, place orders, track deliveries, and shop by photo—all via text message. The feature supports grocery ordering, gift recommendations, and learns preferences over time. It launches to a small group first and will expand to millions in coming weeks. The rollout comes after Amazon blocked Meta's Muse AI agent from querying its site in September.
stories.opinion: A shrewd defensive play: Amazon blocked a rival's shopping agent then launched its own, ensuring it controls the AI-mediated shopping experience on its platform. Timing it before holiday season maximizes adoption pressure. Where coverage differs: TechCrunch emphasizes the Meta Muse blocking context and holiday timing; The Verge focuses more on feature details like grocery ordering and preference learning

stories.title: US tech stocks open higher after worst session in 19 months
stories.summary: US tech stocks opened higher on Wall Street following their worst single-day decline in 19 months, driven by AI-related panic after midterm results. Despite the sharp selloff, the Nasdaq Composite remains up 4.6% for the year, though still more than 10% below peak levels. European and Asia-Pacific markets continued sliding. A stronger-than-expected US jobs report provided support.
stories.opinion: The rebound suggests the selloff was more panic than fundamental repricing, but the 10%-below-peak figure shows the market is still digesting the political risk to AI infrastructure plans.

stories.title: Protesters break into Microsoft data center construction site in Amsterdam
stories.summary: Around 100 protesters from the group Geef Tegengas broke into a Microsoft data center construction site in Amsterdam on November 6, scaling a crane to hang a 'fuck AI' banner and displaying a 'Microsoft powers genocide' banner with 'free Palestine' chants. The project involves three 85-meter towers proceeding despite Amsterdam's ban on new data centers until 2030, as it predates the ban. The action coincides with other activist actions at Microsoft facilities including a mock Israeli military checkpoint outside a Dublin data center.
stories.opinion: This escalation from planned protests to physical site break-ins signals that the European anti-data-center movement is intensifying beyond symbolic demonstrations. The regulatory loophole angle—project approved before the ban—will fuel further backlash.

stories.title: OpenAI drops NDAs for data center projects in post-midterm pivot
stories.summary: OpenAI announced new commitments for its data center projects following midterm elections where voters opposed data center expansion. Key changes include dropping NDAs with public officials (allowing only narrow security and trade-secret protections), paying full electricity and infrastructure costs, publishing expected job creation numbers, and establishing 'local compacts' for each compute campus. Amazon made a similar move in October.
stories.opinion: The timing—right after midterms punished data center expansion—makes this clearly reactive rather than proactive. The NDA retreat and cost-absorption pledges are meaningful concessions that acknowledge the political landscape has shifted against Big Tech infrastructure.

stories.title: METR finds Anthropic's AI progress running 2x faster, with AI driving 80% of speedup
stories.summary: AI-evaluation nonprofit METR published findings from 11 weeks of inside access to Anthropic, estimating the company's AI progress is running roughly 2x faster than its 2024-25 pace, with AI itself responsible for about 80% of the acceleration. METR found no clear bottlenecks to slow this trend. The report revealed two internal models ahead of publicly available Claude Opus 5.5, including a 'Model 4' that cleared 50% on all 15 tested benchmarks. Anthropic heavily redacted the strongest evidence. Anthropic's own IPO filing defined a danger threshold as 'dramatically accelerated progress attributable to AI,' and METR's findings suggest that point may be approaching.
stories.opinion: This is the most consequential AI governance disclosure in months. An independent evaluator confirming recursive self-improvement at 2x pace—with AI doing most of the work—puts Anthropic's own stated danger threshold in play. The heavy redactions suggest the full picture is even more striking.

stories.title: Decade-old 'sshole' vulnerability lets attackers SSH into Linux devices without a password
stories.summary: A decade-old vulnerability nicknamed 'sshole' allows attackers to log into Linux devices via SSH without any password by entering more than 256 characters in the password field. It affects systems running OpenSSH with musl libc without PAM, most notably Alpine Linux. The root cause is disputed between OpenSSH and musl developers, though both have issued patches. Impact is potentially large given Alpine's widespread use in containers (over 1 billion Docker Hub downloads), embedded devices, routers, and IoT, many of which are difficult to update.
stories.opinion: The simplicity of exploitation—just type a long password—combined with Alpine's massive container footprint makes this a high-urgency patching event. The finger-pointing between OpenSSH and musl is concerning because it suggests the bug class may recur.

stories.title: Google DeepMind launches Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash with 15-second clips and 30% price cut
stories.summary: Google DeepMind announced Gemini Omni 1.2 Flash, extending video clip length to 15 seconds, improving reference adherence and consistency, adding multi-turn conversational editing for iterative adjustments, and reducing pricing by 30%. The model is generally available via the Gemini API, Google Vids, and Gemini for business, targeting professional video content production at scale.
stories.opinion: The 30% price reduction alongside capability improvements signals Google is competing aggressively on video generation economics, likely pressuring OpenAI's Sora and other competitors on the cost dimension that matters most for enterprise adoption.

stories.title: Tau Robotics sends remotely piloted humanoid robots to clean San Francisco homes for $60/week
stories.summary: MIT Technology Review tested Tau Robotics' new humanoid-robot cleaning service in San Francisco. The startup sends remotely piloted four-and-a-half-foot-tall humanoid robots to clean homes for $60/week or $100 for a one-time visit. The robots have 3D-printed claw hands and wear grippy socks. While physically capable, they are slow and require significant human guidance—many tasks use kinematic guidance where a human pilot's movements are mirrored. Some tasks like vacuuming can be done autonomously. The real business model is data collection: every session generates training data to eventually build fully autonomous cleaning robots.
stories.opinion: This is a clever data flywheel disguised as a cleaning service—customers pay to generate the training data that will eventually replace the human pilots. The $60/week price point is competitive enough with human cleaners to sustain the model while the autonomy improves.

stories.title: Pew survey finds Americans' trust in news organizations rising across party lines
stories.summary: A Pew Research Center survey finds trust in national news organizations rose from 56% to 62% and trust in local news from 70% to 75% over the past year. Increases span both parties, though Democrats remain more trusting overall. Trust in social media as an information source remains lower. The newsletter also notes Trump blaming Fox News for Republican midterm losses, with 57% of Republicans regularly getting news from Fox News per a 2025 survey.
stories.opinion: The bipartisan trust increase is notable given the polarized media environment. The Trump-Fox tension after midterm losses could disrupt the tight alignment between conservative media and Republican messaging.

stories.title: White-collar workers quitting jobs over AI fears despite no evidence of mass layoffs
stories.summary: A growing trend of white-collar workers are quitting their jobs due to fears about AI disruption. The article highlights Mrinank Sharma, an AI researcher who left Anthropic and posted a widely-viewed resignation letter on X warning of a world 'in peril' from AI, before pursuing a poetry degree. While there's no evidence linking AI to mass layoffs, the technology has already 'changed worker psychology.'
stories.opinion: The psychological impact running ahead of actual job losses is a significant phenomenon—AI anxiety is reshaping career decisions even without material displacement. The Anthropic researcher's exit is particularly striking as an insider signal.

stories.title: Startup Underdog demos 32MB text-to-speech model that runs entirely in the browser
stories.summary: AI startup Underdog demoed Woof, a 32MB (31 million parameters) text-to-speech model that runs entirely in the browser without internet. The company showcased it through an interactive retro-themed game. The open model follows Underdog's recent Bark release, a 167MB speech-to-text model also for edge devices. Founded by Sigil Wen, Underdog focuses on AI models small enough for consumer devices, emphasizing data privacy and open, American-made models.
stories.opinion: A 32MB speech model running in-browser is a meaningful technical achievement that could enable a new class of offline-first voice applications. The privacy angle is increasingly compelling as cloud AI providers face scrutiny over data practices.

stories.title: Guardian asks teachers and parents about AI-generated school emails
stories.summary: The Guardian is soliciting experiences from teachers and parents about the growing use of AI tools like ChatGPT and Claude to draft emails in school-home communications, asking whether school leaders have noticed AI-generated parent emails and what impact this has had.
stories.opinion: This is a callout for reader responses rather than a reported story, but it signals that AI-mediated communication in everyday institutional settings is becoming visible enough to warrant journalistic attention.

stories.title: Physicl raises $10M to build high-fidelity 3D environments for robot training
stories.summary: Physicl, founded by Alex de Vigan (previously of nfinite), raised $10M in seed funding from Inovia Capital to repurpose e-commerce 3D rendering technology for robotics training. The company addresses the sim-to-real gap by transforming real-world information into 3D physical representations with correct geometry, materials, and physics. Their Studio product offers 10,000 3D environments and 100,000 object assets for generating synthetic training data, focusing on difficult edge cases.
stories.opinion: The e-commerce-to-robotics pivot is smart—3D rendering for product visualization and 3D rendering for robot training share core technical requirements but the robotics market has far higher growth potential.

tweet_headlines.author: Michael_Fenech_
tweet_headlines.headline: Michael Fenech found that iterating on Grok Bot instructions without pruning quietly __inflates instruction length and cost__ with every update.
tweet_headlines.source_text:
I found a hidden problem in my Grok Bot setup that could be lurking in yours too.

Every improvement was potentially making my routines more expensive to run.

Before I give you the prompt and solution, here's what I discovered:

I've been experimenting with a research routine, constantly refining its instructions to improve the results.

But I noticed a problem.

Some updates were replacing old instructions. Others were simply adding new ones on top.

That meant Grok Bot was sometimes reading outdated rules alongside the new ones on every run.

More instructions. More usage. Potentially conflicting rules.

Here's the 6-step process I'm now using to prevent this.

Paste this into your Grok Bot Chief of Staff:

"From now on, whenever I ask you to update a Bot, routine, skill or instruction file, follow this process:

1: REPLACE, DON'T ADD. Update the existing rule instead of stacking new instructions on top of old ones.

2: FIND CONFLICTS. Search accessible Bots, routines, skills and instruction files for outdated or contradictory versions of the rule.

3: ARCHIVE OLD VERSIONS. Propose moving superseded files into a dated archive outside the active instructions. Never delete or archive anything without my approval.

4: KEEP ONE SOURCE OF TRUTH. Maintain a version index identifying the current instruction files and which Bots or routines use them.

5: VERIFY WHAT LOADS. After an approved change, check the instructions and files the affected Bot or routine actually uses. Flag anything you cannot inspect.

6: REPORT THE CHANGE. Show me what was replaced, what remains active, any conflicts found and what still needs approval.

Also propose a monthly audit to identify duplicated, outdated or conflicting instructions across my setup. Do not schedule it without my approval."

The lesson: Improving your Grok Bot instructions shouldn't mean endlessly adding more instructions.

Sometimes the biggest upgrade is removing the rules your Bots no longer need.
